nodes.name: unconstrained minimization over Euclidean space
nodes.statement: Formally, the problem of unconstrained optimization is stated in general terms as that of finding the minimum value that a function attains over Euclidean space, i.e. $$ \mathop{\text{min}}_{x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}}f(x). $$
nodes.statement_short: Find $\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n} f(x)$, the unconstrained minimum of $f$ over Euclidean space.

nodes.name: condition number
nodes.statement: Let $\kappa$ be the condition number, which is the ratio of the smallest eigenvalue and the largest eigenvalue of Hessian at local minima.
nodes.genus: the ratio of the smallest eigenvalue and the largest eigenvalue

nodes.name: phase space
nodes.statement: The concept of phase space, developed in the late 19th century, usually consists of all possible values of position and momentum variables.

nodes.name: energy function $H(x,v)$
nodes.statement: the energy function $H(x,v) = \frac{1}{2}\|v\|^{2} + f(x)$

nodes.name: gradient method
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \left\{\begin{aligned} & x_{k+1} = x_{k} - h \nabla f(x_{k})\\ & \text{Any Initial Point}: \; x_{0}. \end{aligned}\right. \end{equation}

nodes.name: momentum method (Polyak heavy ball method)
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \left\{\begin{aligned} & x_{k+1} = x_{k} - h \nabla f(x_{k}) + \gamma_{k} (x_{k} - x_{k-1})\\ & \text{Any Initial Point}: \; x_{0}. \end{aligned}\right. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Nesterov's accelerated gradient method
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \left\{\begin{aligned} & y_{k+1} = x_{k} - \frac{1}{L} \nabla f(x_{k}) \\ & x_{k+1} = x_{k} + \gamma_{k}(x_{k+1} - x_{k})\\ & \text{Any Initial Point}: \; x_{0} = y_{0} \end{aligned}\right. \end{equation} where the parameter is set as $$ \gamma_{k} = \frac{\alpha_{k} (1 - \alpha_{k})}{\alpha_{k}^{2} + \alpha_{k+1}}\quad \text{and}\quad \alpha_{k+1}^{2} = (1 - \alpha_{k+1})\alpha_{k}^{2} + \alpha_{k+1} \kappa. $$
nodes.statement_short: Nesterov's two-sequence accelerated scheme with parameter recursion for $\gamma_k,\alpha_k$.

nodes.name: gradient system (continuous-time limit of the gradient method)
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \left\{\begin{aligned} & \dot{x} = - \nabla f(x_{k})\\ & x(0)= x_{0}, \end{aligned}\right. \end{equation}

nodes.name: second-order ODE with friction
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \left\{\begin{aligned} & \ddot{x} + \gamma_{t} \dot{x} + \nabla f(x) = 0\\ & x(0)= x_{0}, \;\dot{x}(0) =0, \end{aligned}\right. \end{equation}

nodes.name: governing motion equation in a conservation force field
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \left\{\begin{aligned} & \ddot{x} = - \nabla f(x) \\ & x(0)= x_{0}, \;\dot{x}(0) =0. \end{aligned}\right. \end{equation}

nodes.name: phase-space form of the conservation motion equation
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \left\{\begin{aligned} & \dot{x} = v \\ & \dot{v} = -\nabla f(x) \\ & x(0)= x_{0}, \;v(0) =0 . \end{aligned}\right. \end{equation}

nodes.name: analytical solution of the gradient system for $f(x)=\frac{1}{200}x^{2}$
nodes.statement: \begin{numcases}{} x(t) = x_{0}e^{-\frac{1}{100}t} \\ f(x(t)) = \frac{1}{200}x_{0}^{2} e^{-\frac{1}{50}t}. \end{numcases}
nodes.statement_short: Exponential decay $x(t)=x_0e^{-t/100}$ with $f$ decaying at rate $e^{-t/50}$.

nodes.name: analytical solution of the friction system with optimal friction parameter
nodes.statement: \begin{numcases}{} x(t) = x_{0}\left(1 + \frac{1}{10}t \right)e^{-\frac{1}{10}t} \\ f(x(t)) = \frac{1}{200}x_{0}^{2} \left(1 + \frac{1}{10}t \right)^{2} e^{-\frac{1}{5}t}. \end{numcases}
nodes.statement_short: Critically damped solution $x(t)=x_0(1+t/10)e^{-t/10}$ for $\gamma_t=1/5$.

nodes.name: analytical solution of the conservation system
nodes.statement: \begin{numcases}{} x(t) = x_{0}\cos\left(\frac{1}{10}t\right)\quad \text{and}\quad v(t) = x_{0}\sin\left(\frac{1}{10}t\right) \\ f(x(t)) = \frac{1}{200}x_{0}^{2} \cos^{2}\left(\frac{1}{10}t\right) \end{numcases}
nodes.statement_short: Undamped oscillation $x(t)=x_0\cos(t/10)$, $v(t)=x_0\sin(t/10)$.

nodes.name: first-order symplectic Euler scheme
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \left\{\begin{aligned} & x_{k+1} = x_{k} + h v_{k+1} \\ & v_{k+1} = v_{k} - h \nabla f(x_{k}) \end{aligned}\right. \end{equation}
nodes.origin_citation: symplectic Euler method for Hamiltonian systems

nodes.name: St\"{o}rmer-Verlet scheme
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \left\{\begin{aligned} & v_{k+1/2} = v_{k} - \frac{h}{2}\nabla f(x_{k}) \\ & x_{k+1} = x_{k} + h v_{k + 1/2} \\ & v_{k+1} = v_{k + 1/2} - \frac{h}{2} \nabla f(x_{k+1}) \end{aligned}\right. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Second-order symmetric half-step velocity update preserving left-right symmetry.

nodes.name: leap-frog (2nd-order ODE) discretization
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} x_{k+1} - 2x_{k} + x_{k-1} = -h^{2}\nabla f(x_{k}) \end{equation}

nodes.name: translated symplectic Euler scheme at a local minimum
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \left\{ \begin{aligned} &y_{k+1} = y_{k} + hv_{k+1} \\ &v_{k+1} = v_{k} - h\nabla f(x^{\star} + y_{k}), \end{aligned} \right. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Symplectic Euler rewritten in the shifted variable $y_k=x_k-x^\star$.

nodes.name: locally linearized symplectic Euler scheme
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \left\{ \begin{aligned} &y_{k+1} = y_{k} + hv_{k+1} \\ &v_{k+1} = v_{k} - h\nabla^{2} f(x^{\star})y_{k}. \end{aligned} \right. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Linearization of the shifted scheme with $\nabla f$ replaced by $\nabla^2 f(x^\star)y_k$.

nodes.name: block-diagonalized (per-eigendirection) iteration
nodes.statement: From Lemma~\ref{lem:symmetric}, we know that the equation~(\ref{eqn:equiv}) can be written as the equivalent form \begin{equation} \begin{pmatrix} (U_{1}^{T}y)_{k+1,i} \\ (U_{1}^{T}v)_{k+1,i} \end{pmatrix} =T_{i} \begin{pmatrix} (U_{1}^{T}y)_{k,i} \\ (U_{1}^{T}v)_{k,i} \end{pmatrix}= \begin{pmatrix} 1-\omega_{i}^{2}h^{2} & h \\ -\omega_{i}^{2}h &1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} (U_{1}^{T}y)_{k,i} \\ (U_{1}^{T}v)_{k,i} \end{pmatrix} \end{equation} where $i = 1, \ldots, n$.
nodes.statement_short: In the eigenbasis the iteration decouples into $n$ independent $2\times2$ maps $T_i$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Some Lemmas For The Linearized Scheme

nodes.name: coordinate transformation $\theta_{i}, \phi_{i}$
nodes.statement: Let $\theta_{i}$ and $\phi_{i}$ for $i = 1,\ldots,n$ for the new coordinate variables as below \begin{equation} \left\{\begin{aligned} & \cos\theta_{i} = 1-\frac{h^{2}\omega_{i}^{2}}{2} \\ & \sin\theta_{i} = h\omega_{i}\sqrt{1 - \frac{h^{2}\omega_{i}^{2}}{4}} \end{aligned}\right.,\qquad\quad \left\{\begin{aligned} & \cos\phi_{i} = \frac{h\omega_{i}}{2} \\ & \sin\phi_{i} = \sqrt{1 - \frac{h^{2}\omega_{i}^{2}}{4}} \end{aligned}\right. \end{equation} In order to make $\theta_{i}$ and $\phi_{i}$ located in $\left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$, we need to shrink to $0 < h\omega_{i} < \sqrt{2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Angle variables $\theta_i,\phi_i$ encoding the eigenvalues of $T_i$, valid for $0<h\omega_i<\sqrt{2}$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Some Lemmas For The Linearized Scheme

nodes.name: approximated iterative solution for ill-conditioned eigen-directions
nodes.statement: With Assumption~\ref{ass:ill}, the iterative solution~(\ref{eqn:sol}) can be rewritten as \begin{equation} \begin{pmatrix} (U_{1}^{T}y)_{k,i} \\ (U_{1}^{T}v)_{k,i} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \cos(kh\omega_{i}) & \frac{\sin(kh\omega_{i})}{\omega_{i}}\\ -\omega_{i}\sin(kh\omega_{i}) & -\cos(kh\omega_{i}) \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} (U_{1}^{T}y)_{0,i} \\ (U_{1}^{T}v)_{0,i} \end{pmatrix} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Under Assumption A1 the iteration becomes a pure rotation with frequency $h\omega_i$.

nodes.name: local decay ratio of the iterate
nodes.statement: For some $i$ such that $k\omega_{i}h$ approximating $\frac{\pi}{2}$, we have \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \frac{\left|(U_{1}^{T}y)_{k+1,i}\right|}{\left|(U_{1}^{T}y)_{k,i}\right|} & = \frac{\cos\left((k+1)h\omega_{i}\right)}{\cos\left(kh\omega_{i}\right)} \\ & = e^{\ln\cos\left((k+1)h\omega_{i}\right) - \ln \cos\left(kh\omega_{i}\right) } \\ & = e^{-\tan(\xi) h\omega_{i}} \end{aligned} \end{equation} where $\xi \in \left(kh\omega_{i}, (k+1)h\omega_{i}\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Consecutive iterates contract by $e^{-\tan(\xi)h\omega_i}$ with $\xi$ between $kh\omega_i$ and $(k+1)h\omega_i$.

nodes.name: iteration-count estimate for the conservation method
nodes.statement: From the analytical solution for local convex quadratic function with maximum eigenvalue $L$ and minimum eigenvalue $\mu$, in general, the step size by $\frac{1}{\sqrt{L}}$ for momentum method and Nesterov accelerated gradient method, hence the simple estimate for iterative times is approximately $$ n \sim \frac{\pi}{2}\sqrt{\frac{L}{\mu}}. $$ hence, the iterative times $n$ is proportional to the reciprocal of the square root of minimal eigenvalue $\sqrt{\mu}$, which is essentially different from the convergence rate of the gradient method and momentum method.
nodes.statement_short: The number of iterations scales like $\frac{\pi}{2}\sqrt{L/\mu}$, i.e. with $1/\sqrt{\mu}$.
assumptions: local convex quadratic function with maximum eigenvalue $L$ and minimum eigenvalue $\mu$
the step size by $\frac{1}{\sqrt{L}}$ for momentum method and Nesterov accelerated gradient method
conclusions: the iterative times $n$ is proportional to the reciprocal of the square root of minimal eigenvalue $\sqrt{\mu}$

nodes.name: trajectory comparison of the four methods
nodes.statement: A clear fact in figure~\ref{fig:trajectory} shows that the gradient correction decrease the oscillation to comparing with momentum method. A more clear observation is that artificially dissipating method owns the same property with the other three method by the law of nature, that is, if the trajectory come into the local minima in one dimension will not leave it very far. However, from figure~\ref{fig:common} and figure~\ref{fig:diff}, the more rapid convergence rate from artificially dissipating energy method has been shown.
nodes.statement_short: The gradient correction damps oscillation, and the dissipating-energy method keeps the same trajectory property while converging faster.

nodes.name: choice of the initial velocity in Algorithm 2
nodes.statement: In the algorithm~\ref{alg:global}, we can set $v_{0} > 0$ such that the total energy large enough to climb up some high peak. Same as the algorithm~\ref{alg:local}, the function value $f(x)$ is not need in the while loop in order to speed up the computation.
nodes.section: 3.2 Energy Conservation Algorithm For Detecting Local Minima

nodes.name: the energy conservation algorithm cannot detect saddle points
nodes.statement: We point out that for the energy conservation algorithm for detecting local minima along the trajectory cannot detect saddle point in the sense of almost everywhere, since the saddle point in original function $f(x)$ is also a saddle point for the energy function $H(x,v) = \frac{1}{2}\|v\|^{2} + f(x)$. The proof process is fully the same in~\citep{lee2016gradient}.
nodes.statement_short: Saddle points of $f$ remain saddle points of $H(x,v)$, so they are avoided almost everywhere.

nodes.name: the combined algorithm cannot guarantee global minima
nodes.statement: We remark that the combined algorithm (algorithm~\ref{alg:combined}) cannot guarantee to find global minima if the initial position is not ergodic. The tracking local minima is dependent on the trajectory. However, the time of computation and precision based on the proposed algorithm is far better than the large sampled gradient method. Our proposed algorithm first makes the global minima found become possible.
nodes.statement_short: Global optimality is not guaranteed since tracking depends on the trajectory and initial ergodicity.

nodes.name: justification of the local linearized analysis
nodes.statement: The local linearized analysis is based on the stability theorem in finite dimension, the invariant stable manifold theorem and Hartman-Grobman linearized map theorem~\citep{hartman1982ordinary}. The thought is firstly used in~\citep{polyak1964some} to estimate the local convergence of momentum method. And in the paper~\citep{lee2016gradient}, the thought is used to exclude the possiblity to converegnce to saddle point. However, the two theorems above belong to the qualitative theorem of ODE. Hence, the linearized scheme~(\ref{eqn:equiv_linear}) is only an approximate estimate for the original scheme~(\ref{eqn:equiv_sym}) locally.
nodes.statement_short: Linearization is justified only qualitatively, by the stable-manifold and Hartman-Grobman theorems.
nodes.section: 4 An Asymptotic Analysis for The Phenomena of Local High-Speed Convergence

nodes.name: step size conditions $0<hL<2$ and $0<hL<1$
nodes.statement: Here, the behavior is similar as the thought in~\citep{lee2016gradient}. The step size $0<hL<2$ make sure the global convergence of gradient method. And the step size $0<hL<1$ make the uniqueness of the trajectory along the gradient method, the thought of which is equivalent of the existencen and uniqueness of the solution for ODE. Actually, the step size $0<hL<1$ owns the property with the solution of ODE, the continous-limit version. A global existence of the solution for gradient system is proved in~\citep{perko2013differential}.
nodes.statement_short: The smaller step-size condition $0<hL<1$ mirrors existence-uniqueness for the limiting ODE.

nodes.name: Artifically Dissipating Energy Algorithm
nodes.statement: \begin{algorithm}[H] \begin{algorithmic}[1] \State{Given a starting point $x_{0} \in \mathbf{dom}(f)$} \State{Initialize the step length $h$, $\text{maxiter}$, and the velocity variable $v_{0} = 0$} \State{Initialize the iterative variable $v_{iter} = v_{0}$} \While{$\|\nabla f(x)\| > \epsilon$\;and\; $k < \text{maxiter}$} \State{Compute $v_{iter}$ from the below equation in~(\ref{eqn:symplectic_euler})} \If{$\|v_{iter}\| \leq \|v\|$} \State{$v = 0$} \Else \State{$v = v_{iter}$} \EndIf \State{Compute $x$ from the above equation in~(\ref{eqn:symplectic_euler})} \State{$x_k = x$;} \State{$f(x_{k}) = f(x)$;} \State{$k = k + 1$;} \EndWhile \end{algorithmic} \caption{Artifically Dissipating Energy Algorithm} \end{algorithm}
nodes.statement_short: Iterate symplectic Euler on $\ddot x=-\nabla f(x)$ and reset the velocity to zero whenever its norm stops increasing.
input: \State{Initialize the step length $h$, $\text{maxiter}$, and the velocity variable $v_{0} = 0$}

nodes.name: Energy Conservation Algorithm
nodes.statement: \begin{algorithm}[H] \begin{algorithmic}[1] \State{Given a starting point $x_{0} \in \mathbf{dom}(f)$} \State{Initialize the step size $h$ and the maxiter} \State{Initialize the velocity $v_{0}>0$ and compute $f(x_{0})$} \State{Compute the velocity $x_1$ and $v_{1}$ from the equation~(\ref{eqn:symplectic_euler}), and compute $f(x_1)$ } \For{$k= 1: n$} \State{Compute $x_{k+1}$ and $v_{k+1}$ from~(\ref{eqn:symplectic_euler})} \State{Compute $f(x_{k+1})$} \If{$\|v_{k}\| \geq \|v_{k+1}\|$ and $\|v_{k}\| \geq \|v_{k-1}\|$ } \State{Record the position $x_{k}$} \EndIf \EndFor \end{algorithmic} \caption{Energy Conservation Algorithm} \end{algorithm}
nodes.statement_short: Run the frictionless symplectic iteration with $v_0>0$ and record positions where the velocity norm is a local maximum, marking local minima along the trajectory.
nodes.section: 3.2 Energy Conservation Algorithm For Detecting Local Minima
input: \State{Initialize the step size $h$ and the maxiter}

nodes.name: Combined Algorithm
nodes.statement: \begin{algorithm}[H] \begin{algorithmic}[1] \State{Given some starting points $x_{0,i} \in \mathbf{dom}(f)$ with $i = 1, \ldots,n$} \State{Implement algorithm~\ref{alg:global} detecting the position there exists local minima, noted as $x_{j}$ with $j = 1, \ldots,m$} \State{Implement algorithm~\ref{alg:local} from the result on line $2$ finding the local minima, noted as $x_{k}$ with $k=1,\ldots, l$} \State{Comparison of $f(x_{k})$ with $k=1,\ldots,l$ to find global minima.} \end{algorithmic} \caption{Combined Algorithm} \end{algorithm}
nodes.statement_short: Detect candidate local minima with the energy conservation algorithm, refine each with the dissipating energy algorithm, then take the best function value.
output: \State{Comparison of $f(x_{k})$ with $k=1,\ldots,l$ to find global minima.}

nodes.name: ill-conditioned convex quadratic $f(x_1,x_2)=\frac{1}{2}(x_1^{2}+\alpha x_2^{2})$
nodes.statement: Here, we use a simple convex quadratic function with ill-conditioned eigenvalue for illustration as below, \begin{equation} f(x_1, x_{2}) = \frac{1}{2}\left(x_{1}^{2} + \alpha x_{2}^{2}\right), \end{equation} of which the maximum eigenvalue is $L=1$ and the minimum eigenvalue is $\mu = \alpha$. Hence the scale of the step size for~(\ref{eqn:artifical1}) is $$ \frac{1}{L} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{L}} = 1. $$
nodes.statement_short: A 2-D quadratic with eigenvalues $L=1$ and $\mu=\alpha$, used to compare convergence rates.

nodes.name: piecewise-cosine nonconvex 1-D function
nodes.statement: Here, we use the non-convex function for illustration as below, \begin{equation} f(x) = \left\{\begin{aligned} & 2\cos(x), && x \in [0,2\pi] \\ & \cos(x) + 1, && x \in [2\pi, 4\pi] \\ & 3\cos(x) -1, && x \in [4\pi, 6\pi] \end{aligned}\right. \end{equation} which is the 2nd-order smooth function but not 3rd-order smooth. The maximum eigenvalue can be calculated as below $$ \max\limits_{x\in [0,6\pi]} |f''(x)| = 3. $$ then, the step length is set $h \sim \sqrt{\frac{1}{L}}$. We illustrate that the algorithm~\ref{alg:global} simulate the trajectory and find the local minima in figure~\ref{fig:noncon1}.
nodes.statement_short: A 2nd-order smooth piecewise-cosine function on $[0,6\pi]$ with several local minima.

nodes.name: 2-D potential function with sinusoidal coupling
nodes.statement: Another 2D potential function is shown as below, \begin{equation} f(x_1,x_2) = \frac{1}{2} \left[\left(x_1 - 4\right)^{2} + \left(x_2 - 4\right)^{2} + 8\sin(x_1 + 2x_2)\right]. \end{equation} which is the smooth function with domain in $(x_{1},x_{2}) \in [0,8]\times [0,8]$. The maximum eigenvalue can be calculated as below $$ \max\limits_{x\in [0,6\pi]} |\lambda(f''(x))| \geq 16. $$ then, the step length is set $h \sim \sqrt{\frac{1}{L}}$. We illustrate that the algorithm~\ref{alg:global} simulate the trajectory and find the local minima in figure~\ref{fig:noncon2}.
nodes.statement_short: A smooth 2-D potential on $[0,8]^2$ combining a quadratic bowl with $8\sin(x_1+2x_2)$.

nodes.name: strongly convex quadratic experiment
nodes.statement: Here, we investigate the artificially dissipating energy algorithm (algorithm~\ref{alg:local}) for the strongly convex function for comparison with gradient method, momentum method and Nesterov accelerated gradient method (strongly convex case) by the quadratic function as below. \begin{equation} f(x) = \frac{1}{2}x^{T} Ax + b^{T}x \end{equation} where $A$ is symmetric and positive-definite matrix. The two cases are shown as below: \begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{(\alph*)}] \item The generative matrix $A$ is $500\times 500$ random positive definite matrix with eigenvalue from $1e-6$ to $1$ with one defined eigenvalue $1e-6$. The generative vector $b$ follows i.i.d. Gaussian distribution with mean $0$ and variance $1$. \item The generative matrix $A$ is the notorious example in Nesterov's book~\citep{nesterov2013introductory}, i.e., $$ A = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 & & &&\\ -1 &2 &-1& &&\\ &-1 & 2 &\ddots &&\\ & &\ddots &\ddots &\ddots & \\ & & &\ddots &\ddots &-1 \\ & & & & -1 &2 \end{pmatrix} $$ the eigenvalues of the matrix are $$ \lambda_{k} = 2 - 2\cos\left(\frac{k\pi}{n+1}\right) = 4\sin^{2}\left(\frac{k\pi}{2(n+1)}\right) $$ and $n$ is the dimension of the matrix $A$. The eigenvector can be solved by the second Chebyshev's polynomial. We implement $\dim(A) = 1000$ and $b$ is zero vector. Hence, the smallest eigenvalue is approximating $$ \lambda_{1} = 4\sin^{2}\left(\frac{\pi}{2(n+1)}\right) \approx \frac{\pi^{2}}{1001^{2}} \approx 10^{-5} $$ \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Two ill-conditioned quadratics: a random $500\times500$ PD matrix and Nesterov's tridiagonal example in dimension $1000$.

nodes.name: log-sum-exp non-strongly convex experiment
nodes.statement: Here, we investigate the artificially dissipating energy algorithm (algorithm~\ref{alg:local}) for the non-strongly convex function for comparison with gradient method, Nesterov accelerated gradient method (non-strongly convex case) by the log-sum-exp function as below. \begin{equation} f(x) = \rho \log \left[\sum_{i=1}^{n}\exp\left( \frac{\langle a_{i}, x\rangle - b_{i}}{\rho}\right)\right] \end{equation} where $A$ is the $m\times n$ matrix with $a_{i}$, $(i=1,\ldots,m)$ the column vector of $A$ and $b$ is the $n\times 1$ vector with component $b_{i}$. $\rho$ is the parameter. We show the experiment in~(\ref{eqn:nonstrong}): the matrix $A = \left(a_{ij}\right)_{50\times 200}$ and the vector $b = (b_{i})_{200\times 1}$ are set by the entry following i.i.d Gaussian distribution for the paramter $\rho=5$ and $\rho=10$.
nodes.statement_short: Minimizing a random $50\times200$ log-sum-exp function for $\rho=5$ and $\rho=10$.

nodes.name: Styblinski-Tang function
nodes.statement: Firstly, we investigate Styblinski-Tang function, i.e. \begin{equation} f(x) = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{d} \left(x_{i}^{4} - 16x_{i}^{2} + 5x_{i}\right) \end{equation} to demonstrate the general performance of the algorithm~\ref{alg:global} to track the number of local minima and then find the local minima by algorithm~\ref{alg:combined}.
nodes.statement_short: Classical separable nonconvex test function used to count and locate local minima.
nodes.origin_citation: Styblinski-Tang; virtual library of simulation experiments (Surjanovic & Bingham)

nodes.name: Shekel function
nodes.statement: Furthermore, we demonstrate the numerical experiment from Styblinski-Tang function to more complex Shekel function \begin{equation} f(x) = - \sum_{i=1}^{m} \left(\sum_{j=1}^{4}\left(x_{j} - C_{ji}\right)^{2} + \beta_{i}\right)^{-1} \end{equation} where $$\beta = \frac{1}{10}\left(1, 2, 2, 4, 4, 6, 3, 7, 5, 5\right)^{T}$$ and $$ C = \begin{pmatrix} 4.0 & 1.0 & 8.0 & 6.0 & 3.0 & 2.0 & 5.0 & 8.0 & 6.0 & 7.0 \\ 4.0 & 1.0 & 8.0 & 6.0 & 7.0 & 9.0 & 3.0 & 1.0 & 2.0 & 3.6 \\ 4.0 & 1.0 & 8.0 & 6.0 & 3.0 & 2.0 & 5.0 & 8.0 & 6.0 & 7.0 \\ 4.0 & 1.0 & 8.0 & 6.0 & 7.0 & 9.0 & 3.0 & 1.0 & 2.0 & 3.6 \end{pmatrix}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Classical 4-D multi-well Shekel test function with parameters $\beta$ and $C$.
nodes.origin_citation: Shekel; virtual library of simulation experiments (Surjanovic & Bingham)

nodes.name: Assumption A1 (ill-conditioned eigenvalue approximation)
nodes.statement: If the step size $h = \frac{1}{\sqrt{L}}$ for~(\ref{eqn:equiv_linear}), for the ill-conditioned eigenvalue $\omega_{i} \ll \sqrt{L}$, the coordinate variable can be approximated by the analytical solution as \begin{equation} \theta_{i} = h\omega_{i}, \qquad \text{and}\qquad\phi_{i} = \frac{\pi}{2}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: For $h=1/\sqrt{L}$ and $\omega_i\ll\sqrt{L}$, take $\theta_i\approx h\omega_i$ and $\phi_i\approx\pi/2$.

nodes.name: matrix form of the linearized symplectic-Euler scheme
nodes.statement: The numerical scheme, shown as below \begin{equation} \begin{pmatrix} y_{k+1} \\ v_{k+1} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} I -h^{2}A & hI \\ -hA & I \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} y_{k} \\ v_{k} \end{pmatrix} \end{equation} is equivalent to the linearized symplectic-Euler scheme~(\ref{eqn:equiv_linear}), where we note that the linear transformation is \begin{equation} M =\begin{pmatrix} I -h^{2}A & hI \\ -hA & I \end{pmatrix}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The linearized symplectic Euler iteration is the single linear map $M=\begin{pmatrix}I-h^2A & hI\\ -hA & I\end{pmatrix}$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Some Lemmas For The Linearized Scheme
assumptions: \begin{equation} \begin{pmatrix} y_{k+1} \\ v_{k+1} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} I -h^{2}A & hI \\ -hA & I \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} y_{k} \\ v_{k} \end{pmatrix} \end{equation}
conclusions: is equivalent to the linearized symplectic-Euler scheme~(\ref{eqn:equiv_linear})

nodes.name: orthogonal block-diagonalization of $M$
nodes.statement: For every $2n\times 2n$ matrix $M$ in~(\ref{eqn:equivmatrix}), there exists the orthogonal transformation $U_{2n\times 2n}$ such that the matrix $M$ is similar as below \begin{equation} U^{T}MU = \begin{pmatrix} T_{1} & & & \\ &T_{2} & & \\ & &\ddots & \\ & & & T_{n} \end{pmatrix} \end{equation} where $T_{i}$ $(i=1,\ldots, n)$ is $2\times 2$ matrix with the form \begin{equation} T_{i} = \begin{pmatrix} 1-\omega_{i}^{2}h^{2} & h \\ -\omega_{i}^{2}h & 1 \end{pmatrix} \end{equation} where $\omega_{i}^{2}$ is the eigenvalue of the matrix $A$.
nodes.statement_short: An orthogonal $U$ conjugates $M$ into $n$ diagonal $2\times2$ blocks $T_i$ built from the eigenvalues $\omega_i^2$ of $A$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Some Lemmas For The Linearized Scheme
assumptions: where $\omega_{i}^{2}$ is the eigenvalue of the matrix $A$
conclusions: there exists the orthogonal transformation $U_{2n\times 2n}$ such that the matrix $M$ is similar as below \begin{equation} U^{T}MU = \begin{pmatrix} T_{1} & & & \\ &T_{2} & & \\ & &\ddots & \\ & & & T_{n} \end{pmatrix} \end{equation}
where $T_{i}$ $(i=1,\ldots, n)$ is $2\times 2$ matrix with the form \begin{equation} T_{i} = \begin{pmatrix} 1-\omega_{i}^{2}h^{2} & h \\ -\omega_{i}^{2}h & 1 \end{pmatrix} \end{equation}

nodes.name: eigenvalues of $T_{i}$ are complex of modulus one
nodes.statement: For any step size $h$ satisfying $0<h\omega_{i}<2$, the eigenvalues of the matrix $T_{i}$ are complex with absolute value $1$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Some Lemmas For The Linearized Scheme
conclusions: the eigenvalues of the matrix $T_{i}$ are complex with absolute value $1$

nodes.name: trigonometric relations between $\theta_{i}$ and $\phi_{i}$
nodes.statement: With the new coordinate in~(\ref{eqn:coortran}) for $0 < h\omega_{i} < \sqrt{2}$, we have \begin{equation} 2\phi_{i} + \theta_{i} = \pi \end{equation} and \begin{equation} \left\{\begin{aligned} & \sin\theta_{i} = \sin(2\phi_{i}) = h\omega_{i} \sin\phi_{i}\\ & \sin(3\phi_{i}) = - \left(1 - h^{2}\omega_{i}^{2}\right)\sin\phi_{i} \end{aligned}\right. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The angles satisfy $2\phi_i+\theta_i=\pi$, $\sin(2\phi_i)=h\omega_i\sin\phi_i$ and $\sin(3\phi_i)=-(1-h^2\omega_i^2)\sin\phi_i$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Some Lemmas For The Linearized Scheme
assumptions: With the new coordinate in~(\ref{eqn:coortran}) for $0 < h\omega_{i} < \sqrt{2}$

nodes.name: spectral factorization of $T_{i}$
nodes.statement: With the new coordinate in~(\ref{eqn:coortran}), the matrix $T_{i}$ ($i = 1, \ldots, n$) in~(\ref{eqn:2by2}) can expressed as below, \begin{equation} T_{i} = \frac{1}{\omega_{i} \left(e^{-i\phi_{i}} - e^{i\phi_{i}}\right)} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ \omega_{i} e^{i\phi_{i}} & \omega_{i} e^{-i\phi_{i}} \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} e^{i\theta_{i}} & 0 \\ 0 & e^{-i\theta_{i}} \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} \omega_{i} e^{-i\phi_{i}} & -1 \\ -\omega_{i} e^{i\phi_{i}} & 1 \end{pmatrix} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $T_i$ diagonalizes as $V\,\mathrm{diag}(e^{i\theta_i},e^{-i\theta_i})\,V^{-1}$ with eigenvectors $(1,\omega_ie^{\pm i\phi_i})^T$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Some Lemmas For The Linearized Scheme
assumptions: With the new coordinate in~(\ref{eqn:coortran}), the matrix $T_{i}$ ($i = 1, \ldots, n$) in~(\ref{eqn:2by2})
conclusions: T_{i} = \frac{1}{\omega_{i} \left(e^{-i\phi_{i}} - e^{i\phi_{i}}\right)} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ \omega_{i} e^{i\phi_{i}} & \omega_{i} e^{-i\phi_{i}} \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} e^{i\theta_{i}} & 0 \\ 0 & e^{-i\theta_{i}} \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} \omega_{i} e^{-i\phi_{i}} & -1 \\ -\omega_{i} e^{i\phi_{i}} & 1 \end{pmatrix}

nodes.name: closed form of the iterative solution after $k$ steps
nodes.statement: Let the initial value $y_{0}$ and $v_{0}$, after the first $k$ steps without reseting the velocity, the iterative solution~(\ref{eqn:equiv_linear}) with the equivalent form~(\ref{eqn:equivtran}) has the form as below \begin{equation} \begin{pmatrix} (U_{1}^{T}y)_{k,i} \\ (U_{1}^{T}v)_{k,i} \end{pmatrix} =T_{i}^{k} \begin{pmatrix} (U_{1}^{T}y)_{0,i} \\ (U_{1}^{T}v)_{0,i} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -\frac{\sin(k\theta_{i} - \phi_{i})}{\sin\phi_{i}} & \frac{\sin (k\theta_{i})}{\omega_{i}\sin\phi_{i}} \\ -\frac{\omega_{i} \sin (k\theta_{i})}{\sin\phi_{i}} & \frac{\sin(k\theta_{i} + \phi_{i})}{\sin\phi_{i}} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} (U_{1}^{T}y)_{0,i} \\ (U_{1}^{T}v)_{0,i} \end{pmatrix} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: After $k$ un-reset steps the iterate is given exactly by a trigonometric matrix in $k\theta_i$ and $\phi_i$.
assumptions: after the first $k$ steps without reseting the velocity
conclusions: the iterative solution~(\ref{eqn:equiv_linear}) with the equivalent form~(\ref{eqn:equivtran}) has the form as below \begin{equation} \begin{pmatrix} (U_{1}^{T}y)_{k,i} \\ (U_{1}^{T}v)_{k,i} \end{pmatrix} =T_{i}^{k} \begin{pmatrix} (U_{1}^{T}y)_{0,i} \\ (U_{1}^{T}v)_{0,i} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -\frac{\sin(k\theta_{i} - \phi_{i})}{\sin\phi_{i}} & \frac{\sin (k\theta_{i})}{\omega_{i}\sin\phi_{i}} \\ -\frac{\omega_{i} \sin (k\theta_{i})}{\sin\phi_{i}} & \frac{\sin(k\theta_{i} + \phi_{i})}{\sin\phi_{i}} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} (U_{1}^{T}y)_{0,i} \\ (U_{1}^{T}v)_{0,i} \end{pmatrix} \end{equation}

nodes.name: velocity-reset time for ill-conditioned eigen-directions
nodes.statement: For every ill-conditioned eigen-direction, with every initial condition $(y_{0},0)^{T}$, if the algorithm~\ref{alg:local} is implemented at $\left\|v_{iter}\right\| \leq \left\|v\right\|$, then there exist an eigenvalue $\omega_{i}^{2}$ such that $$k\omega_{i} h \geq \frac{\pi}{2}.$$
nodes.statement_short: When the dissipating-energy reset triggers, some eigen-direction has already advanced a quarter period, $k\omega_i h \ge \pi/2$.
assumptions: if the algorithm~\ref{alg:local} is implemented at $\left\|v_{iter}\right\| \leq \left\|v\right\|$
conclusions: there exist an eigenvalue $\omega_{i}^{2}$ such that $$k\omega_{i} h \geq \frac{\pi}{2}.$$

nodes.name: proof of the matrix form of the linearized scheme
nodes.statement: \begin{proof} $$ \begin{aligned} &\begin{pmatrix} I & -hI \\ 0 & I \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} y_{k+1} \\ v_{k+1} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} I & 0 \\ -hA & I \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} y_{k} \\ v_{k} \end{pmatrix} \Leftrightarrow \begin{pmatrix} y_{k+1} \\ v_{k+1} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} I-h^{2}A & hI \\ -hA & I \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} y_{k} \\ v_{k} \end{pmatrix} \end{aligned} $$ \end{proof}
nodes.statement_short: Direct left-multiplication by the inverse of the implicit block matrix.
nodes.section: 4.1 Some Lemmas For The Linearized Scheme

nodes.name: proof of the orthogonal block-diagonalization
nodes.statement: \begin{proof} Let $\Lambda$ be the diagonal matrix with the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ as below $$ \Lambda =\begin{pmatrix} \omega^{2}_{1} & & & \\ &\omega^{2}_{2} & & \\ & &\ddots & \\ & & & \omega^{2}_{n} \end{pmatrix}. $$ Since $A$ is positive definite and symmetric, there exists orthogonal matrix $U_{1}$ such that $$ U_{1}^{T}AU_{1} = \Lambda. $$ Let $\Pi$ be the permuation matrix satisfying $$ \Pi_{i,j} = \left\{ \begin{aligned} &1, && j\;\text{odd},\; i=\frac{j+1}{2} \\ &1, && j\;\text{even},\; i=n+\frac{j}{2} \\ &0, && \text{otherwise} \end{aligned} \right. $$ where $i$ is the row index and $j$ is the column index. Then, let $U = \mathbf{diag}(U_{1},U_{1})\Pi$, we have by conjugation $$ \begin{aligned} U^{T}MU & =\Pi^{T} \begin{pmatrix} U_{1}^{T} & \\ & U_{1}^{T}\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}I-h^{2}A & hI \\ -hA & I \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} U_{1} & \\ & U_{1}\end{pmatrix}\Pi \\ & = \Pi^{T} \begin{pmatrix} I-h^2\Lambda & hI \\ -h\Lambda & I \end{pmatrix} \Pi\\ & = \begin{pmatrix} T_{1} & & & \\ &T_{2} & & \\ & &\ddots & \\ & & & T_{n} \end{pmatrix} \end{aligned} $$ \end{proof}
nodes.statement_short: Diagonalize $A$ orthogonally, then conjugate $M$ by $\mathrm{diag}(U_1,U_1)$ and a permutation matrix.
nodes.section: 4.1 Some Lemmas For The Linearized Scheme

nodes.name: proof that the eigenvalues of $T_{i}$ have modulus one
nodes.statement: \begin{proof} For $i = 1, \ldots, n$, we have $$ \left|\lambda I - T_{i}\right| = 0\Leftrightarrow \lambda_{1,2} = 1-\frac{h^{2}\omega_{i}^{2}}{2} \pm h\omega_{i}\sqrt{1 - \frac{h^{2}\omega_{i}^{2}}{4}}. $$ \end{proof}
nodes.statement_short: Solve the characteristic polynomial of the $2\times2$ block directly.
nodes.section: 4.1 Some Lemmas For The Linearized Scheme

nodes.name: proof of the trigonometric relations
nodes.statement: \begin{proof} With Sum-Product identities of trigonometric function, we have $$ \begin{aligned} \sin(\theta_{i} + \phi_{i}) & = \sin\theta_{i} \cos\phi _{i}+ \cos\theta_{i} \sin\phi_{i} \\ & = h\omega_{i}\sqrt{1 - \frac{h^{2}\omega_{i}^{2}}{4}} \cdot \frac{h\omega_{i}}{2} + \left(1-\frac{h^{2}\omega_{i}^{2}}{2}\right) \sqrt{1 - \frac{h^{2}\omega_{i}^{2}}{4}}\\ & = \sqrt{1 - \frac{h^{2}\omega_{i}^{2}}{4}}\\ & = \sin\phi_{i}. \end{aligned} $$ Since $0< h\omega_{i} < 2$, we have $\theta_{i}, \phi_{i} \in \left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$, we can obtain that $$ \theta_{i} + \phi_{i} = \pi - \phi_{i} \Leftrightarrow \theta_{i} = \pi - 2\phi_{i} $$ and with the coordinate transfornation in~(\ref{eqn:coortran}), we have $$ \sin\theta_{i} = h\omega_{i} \sin\phi_{i} \Leftrightarrow \sin(2\phi_{i}) = h\omega_{i} \sin\phi_{i}. $$ Next, we use Sum-Product identities of trigonometric function furthermore, $$ \begin{aligned} \sin(\theta_{i} - \phi_{i}) & = \sin\theta_{i} \cos\phi _{i}- \cos\theta_{i} \sin\phi_{i} \\ & = h\omega_{i}\sqrt{1 - \frac{h^{2}\omega_{i}^{2}}{4}} \cdot \frac{h\omega_{i}}{2} - \left(1-\frac{h^{2}\omega_{i}^{2}}{2}\right) \sqrt{1 - \frac{h^{2}\omega_{i}^{2}}{4}}\\ & = \left(h^{2}\omega_{i}^{2}-1\right)\sqrt{1 - \frac{h^{2}\omega_{i}^{2}}{4}}\\ & = -\left(1-h^{2}\omega_{i}^{2}\right) \sin\phi_{i} \end{aligned} $$ and with $\theta_{i} = \pi - 2\phi_{i}$, we have $$ \sin(3\phi_{i}) = -\left(1-h^{2}\omega_{i}^{2}\right) \sin\phi_{i} $$ \end{proof}
nodes.statement_short: Expand $\sin(\theta_i\pm\phi_i)$ with sum-product identities and identify the resulting expressions.
nodes.section: 4.1 Some Lemmas For The Linearized Scheme

nodes.name: proof of the spectral factorization of $T_{i}$
nodes.statement: \begin{proof} For the coordinate transformation in~(\ref{eqn:coortran}), we have $$ T_{i} \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ \omega_{i}e^{i\phi_{i}} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ \omega_{i}e^{i\phi_{i}} \end{pmatrix} e^{i\theta_{i}} \qquad \text{and}\qquad T_{i} \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ \omega_{i}e^{-i\phi_{i}} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ \omega_{i}e^{-i\phi_{i}} \end{pmatrix} e^{-i\theta_{i}} $$ Hence,~(\ref{eqn:equiv_T}) is proved. \end{proof}
nodes.statement_short: Verify that $(1,\omega_ie^{\pm i\phi_i})^T$ are eigenvectors with eigenvalues $e^{\pm i\theta_i}$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Some Lemmas For The Linearized Scheme

nodes.name: proof of the closed form of the iterative solution
nodes.statement: \begin{proof} With Lemma~\ref{lem:equiv_express} and the coordinate transformation~(\ref{eqn:coortran}), we have $$ \begin{aligned} T_{i}^{k} & =\frac{1}{\omega_{i} \left(e^{-i\phi_{i}} - e^{i\phi_{i}}\right)} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ \omega_{i} e^{i\phi_{i}} & \omega_{i} e^{-i\phi_{i}} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} e^{i\theta_{i}} & 0 \\ 0 & e^{-i\theta_{i}} \end{pmatrix}^{k} \begin{pmatrix} \omega_{i} e^{-i\phi_{i}} & -1 \\ -\omega_{i} e^{i\phi_{i}} & 1 \end{pmatrix}\\ & =\frac{1}{\omega_{i} \left(e^{-i\phi_{i}} - e^{i\phi_{i}}\right)} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ \omega_{i} e^{i\phi_{i}} & \omega_{i} e^{-i\phi_{i}} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \omega e^{i(k\theta_{i} -\phi_{i})} & -e^{ik\theta_{i}} \\ -\omega e^{-i(k\theta_{i} -\phi_{i})} & e^{-ik\theta_{i}} \end{pmatrix} \\ & = \begin{pmatrix} -\frac{\sin(k\theta_{i} - \phi_{i})}{\sin\phi_{i}} & \frac{\sin (k\theta_{i})}{\omega_{i}\sin\phi_{i}} \\ -\frac{\omega_{i} \sin (k\theta_{i})}{\sin\phi_{i}} & \frac{\sin(k\theta_{i} + \phi_{i})}{\sin\phi_{i}} \end{pmatrix} \end{aligned} $$ The proof is complete. \end{proof}
nodes.statement_short: Raise the diagonal factorization to the $k$-th power and simplify with the angle identities.

nodes.name: proof of the velocity-reset time bound
nodes.statement: \begin{proof} When $\left\|v_{iter}\right\| \leq \left\|v\right\|$, then $\left\|U_{1}^{T}v_{iter}\right\| \leq \left\|U_{1}^{T}v\right\|$. While for the $\left\|U_{1}^{T}v\right\|$, we can write in the analytical form, $$ \left\|U_{1}^{T}v\right\| = \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \omega_{i}^{2}(U_{1}y_{0})_{i}^{2}\sin^{2}(kh\omega_{i})} $$ if there is no $k\omega_{i} h < \frac{\pi}{2}$, $\left\|U_{1}^{T}v\right\|$ increase with $k$ increasing. \end{proof}
nodes.statement_short: Write the velocity norm analytically; if every $k\omega_i h<\pi/2$ it would still be increasing, a contradiction with the reset condition.

nodes.name: Introduce the eigenvalue matrix $\Lambda$
nodes.statement: Let $\Lambda$ be the diagonal matrix with the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ as below $$ \Lambda =\begin{pmatrix} \omega^{2}_{1} & & & \\ &\omega^{2}_{2} & & \\ & &\ddots & \\ & & & \omega^{2}_{n} \end{pmatrix}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Name the diagonal matrix of eigenvalues of $A$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Some Lemmas For The Linearized Scheme

nodes.name: Orthogonal diagonalization of $A$
nodes.statement: Since $A$ is positive definite and symmetric, there exists orthogonal matrix $U_{1}$ such that $$ U_{1}^{T}AU_{1} = \Lambda. $$
nodes.statement_short: Invoke the spectral theorem for symmetric positive definite $A$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Some Lemmas For The Linearized Scheme

nodes.name: Construct the permutation matrix $\Pi$
nodes.statement: Let $\Pi$ be the permuation matrix satisfying $$ \Pi_{i,j} = \left\{ \begin{aligned} &1, && j\;\text{odd},\; i=\frac{j+1}{2} \\ &1, && j\;\text{even},\; i=n+\frac{j}{2} \\ &0, && \text{otherwise} \end{aligned} \right. $$ where $i$ is the row index and $j$ is the column index.
nodes.statement_short: Build the odd/even interleaving permutation that groups coordinates into pairs.
nodes.section: 4.1 Some Lemmas For The Linearized Scheme

nodes.name: Conjugate $M$ by $U$
nodes.statement: Then, let $U = \mathbf{diag}(U_{1},U_{1})\Pi$, we have by conjugation $$ \begin{aligned} U^{T}MU & =\Pi^{T} \begin{pmatrix} U_{1}^{T} & \\ & U_{1}^{T}\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}I-h^{2}A & hI \\ -hA & I \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} U_{1} & \\ & U_{1}\end{pmatrix}\Pi \\ & = \Pi^{T} \begin{pmatrix} I-h^2\Lambda & hI \\ -h\Lambda & I \end{pmatrix} \Pi\\ & = \begin{pmatrix} T_{1} & & & \\ &T_{2} & & \\ & &\ddots & \\ & & & T_{n} \end{pmatrix} \end{aligned} $$
nodes.statement_short: Conjugation by $U$ turns $M$ into the block-diagonal matrix of $T_i$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Some Lemmas For The Linearized Scheme

nodes.name: Expand $\sin(\theta_i+\phi_i)$
nodes.statement: With Sum-Product identities of trigonometric function, we have $$ \begin{aligned} \sin(\theta_{i} + \phi_{i}) & = \sin\theta_{i} \cos\phi _{i}+ \cos\theta_{i} \sin\phi_{i} \\ & = h\omega_{i}\sqrt{1 - \frac{h^{2}\omega_{i}^{2}}{4}} \cdot \frac{h\omega_{i}}{2} + \left(1-\frac{h^{2}\omega_{i}^{2}}{2}\right) \sqrt{1 - \frac{h^{2}\omega_{i}^{2}}{4}}\\ & = \sqrt{1 - \frac{h^{2}\omega_{i}^{2}}{4}}\\ & = \sin\phi_{i}. \end{aligned} $$
nodes.statement_short: Sum-product expansion gives $\sin(\theta_i+\phi_i)=\sin\phi_i$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Some Lemmas For The Linearized Scheme

nodes.name: Deduce $\theta_i=\pi-2\phi_i$
nodes.statement: Since $0< h\omega_{i} < 2$, we have $\theta_{i}, \phi_{i} \in \left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$, we can obtain that $$ \theta_{i} + \phi_{i} = \pi - \phi_{i} \Leftrightarrow \theta_{i} = \pi - 2\phi_{i} $$
nodes.statement_short: The angle range forces $\theta_i+\phi_i=\pi-\phi_i$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Some Lemmas For The Linearized Scheme

nodes.name: Substitute to get the $\sin(2\phi_i)$ identity
nodes.statement: and with the coordinate transfornation in~(\ref{eqn:coortran}), we have $$ \sin\theta_{i} = h\omega_{i} \sin\phi_{i} \Leftrightarrow \sin(2\phi_{i}) = h\omega_{i} \sin\phi_{i}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Substituting the coordinate definitions yields $\sin(2\phi_i)=h\omega_i\sin\phi_i$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Some Lemmas For The Linearized Scheme

nodes.name: Expand $\sin(\theta_i-\phi_i)$
nodes.statement: Next, we use Sum-Product identities of trigonometric function furthermore, $$ \begin{aligned} \sin(\theta_{i} - \phi_{i}) & = \sin\theta_{i} \cos\phi _{i}- \cos\theta_{i} \sin\phi_{i} \\ & = h\omega_{i}\sqrt{1 - \frac{h^{2}\omega_{i}^{2}}{4}} \cdot \frac{h\omega_{i}}{2} - \left(1-\frac{h^{2}\omega_{i}^{2}}{2}\right) \sqrt{1 - \frac{h^{2}\omega_{i}^{2}}{4}}\\ & = \left(h^{2}\omega_{i}^{2}-1\right)\sqrt{1 - \frac{h^{2}\omega_{i}^{2}}{4}}\\ & = -\left(1-h^{2}\omega_{i}^{2}\right) \sin\phi_{i} \end{aligned} $$
nodes.statement_short: The difference expansion gives $-(1-h^2\omega_i^2)\sin\phi_i$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Some Lemmas For The Linearized Scheme

nodes.name: Conclude the $\sin(3\phi_i)$ identity
nodes.statement: and with $\theta_{i} = \pi - 2\phi_{i}$, we have $$ \sin(3\phi_{i}) = -\left(1-h^{2}\omega_{i}^{2}\right) \sin\phi_{i} $$
nodes.statement_short: Substituting $\theta_i=\pi-2\phi_i$ gives the third relation.
nodes.section: 4.1 Some Lemmas For The Linearized Scheme

nodes.name: Verify the two eigenvector relations
nodes.statement: For the coordinate transformation in~(\ref{eqn:coortran}), we have $$ T_{i} \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ \omega_{i}e^{i\phi_{i}} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ \omega_{i}e^{i\phi_{i}} \end{pmatrix} e^{i\theta_{i}} \qquad \text{and}\qquad T_{i} \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ \omega_{i}e^{-i\phi_{i}} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ \omega_{i}e^{-i\phi_{i}} \end{pmatrix} e^{-i\theta_{i}} $$
nodes.statement_short: Check that $(1,\omega_ie^{\pm i\phi_i})^T$ are eigenvectors of $T_i$ with eigenvalues $e^{\pm i\theta_i}$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Some Lemmas For The Linearized Scheme

nodes.name: Conclude the factorization
nodes.statement: Hence,~(\ref{eqn:equiv_T}) is proved.
nodes.section: 4.1 Some Lemmas For The Linearized Scheme

nodes.name: Compute $T_i^{k}$
nodes.statement: With Lemma~\ref{lem:equiv_express} and the coordinate transformation~(\ref{eqn:coortran}), we have $$ \begin{aligned} T_{i}^{k} & =\frac{1}{\omega_{i} \left(e^{-i\phi_{i}} - e^{i\phi_{i}}\right)} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ \omega_{i} e^{i\phi_{i}} & \omega_{i} e^{-i\phi_{i}} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} e^{i\theta_{i}} & 0 \\ 0 & e^{-i\theta_{i}} \end{pmatrix}^{k} \begin{pmatrix} \omega_{i} e^{-i\phi_{i}} & -1 \\ -\omega_{i} e^{i\phi_{i}} & 1 \end{pmatrix}\\ & =\frac{1}{\omega_{i} \left(e^{-i\phi_{i}} - e^{i\phi_{i}}\right)} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ \omega_{i} e^{i\phi_{i}} & \omega_{i} e^{-i\phi_{i}} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \omega e^{i(k\theta_{i} -\phi_{i})} & -e^{ik\theta_{i}} \\ -\omega e^{-i(k\theta_{i} -\phi_{i})} & e^{-ik\theta_{i}} \end{pmatrix} \\ & = \begin{pmatrix} -\frac{\sin(k\theta_{i} - \phi_{i})}{\sin\phi_{i}} & \frac{\sin (k\theta_{i})}{\omega_{i}\sin\phi_{i}} \\ -\frac{\omega_{i} \sin (k\theta_{i})}{\sin\phi_{i}} & \frac{\sin(k\theta_{i} + \phi_{i})}{\sin\phi_{i}} \end{pmatrix} \end{aligned} $$
nodes.statement_short: Raise the diagonal middle factor to the $k$-th power and simplify to trigonometric entries.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: The proof is complete.

nodes.name: Transfer the reset condition to the eigenbasis
nodes.statement: When $\left\|v_{iter}\right\| \leq \left\|v\right\|$, then $\left\|U_{1}^{T}v_{iter}\right\| \leq \left\|U_{1}^{T}v\right\|$.
nodes.statement_short: Orthogonal invariance carries the reset inequality into the eigen-coordinates.

nodes.name: Analytical form of the velocity norm
nodes.statement: While for the $\left\|U_{1}^{T}v\right\|$, we can write in the analytical form, $$ \left\|U_{1}^{T}v\right\| = \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \omega_{i}^{2}(U_{1}y_{0})_{i}^{2}\sin^{2}(kh\omega_{i})} $$
nodes.statement_short: Express the velocity norm as a sum of $\sin^2(kh\omega_i)$ terms.

nodes.name: Contradiction with monotone increase
nodes.statement: if there is no $k\omega_{i} h < \frac{\pi}{2}$, $\left\|U_{1}^{T}v\right\|$ increase with $k$ increasing.
nodes.statement_short: Without some $k\omega_i h\ge\pi/2$ the velocity norm would keep growing, contradicting the reset.

nodes.name: rigorous convergence rate for the artificially dissipating energy method
nodes.statement: However, for our artificially dissipating energy method, since there are trigonometric functions from~(\ref{eqn:sol}), we cannot propose the rigorous mathematic proof for the convergence rate. If everybody can propose a theoretical proof, it is very beautiful.
nodes.statement_short: No rigorous convergence-rate proof is known for the dissipating-energy method because of the trigonometric matrix entries.
